Useful time / Honest comparison

Does a faster draft mean a faster job?

Compare the whole task, not just the moment an answer appears. This free calculator includes setup, assisted production, checking, repairs, and upkeep. It shows a loss when the new workflow takes longer.

No AI runs here. The page performs arithmetic on numbers you enter. It does not observe your work, check your output, or predict productivity.

Worked arithmetic / Not measured outcomes
Three examples, including when not to repeat it.
These inputs are fictional teaching examples, not results from Nolan or claims about any AI service.


A repeated task eventually recovers setup.
Usual effort: 30 minutes. Assisted production: 8 minutes. Review and repair: 7 minutes. Six repetitions, 60 minutes of setup, and 15 minutes of upkeep.
Usual total: 180 minutes. Assisted total: 165 minutes. Net saving: 15 minutes. The per-task difference is 15 minutes, against 75 minutes of overhead. Five repetitions exactly recover that overhead; positive savings start at six. Quality still needs checking.


A one-off task can lose time.
Use the same 30, 8, and 7 minutes, but do the task once, with 60 minutes of setup and no upkeep.
Usual total: 30 minutes. Assisted total: 75 minutes. Extra effort: 45 minutes. A quicker draft does not recover the setup. A one-off task may be better handled by the simpler method.


Review can cost more than production saves.
Usual effort: 20 minutes. Assisted production: 5 minutes. Review and repair: 18 minutes. Ten repetitions, 10 minutes of setup, and 5 minutes of upkeep.
Usual total: 200 minutes. Assisted total: 245 minutes. Extra effort: 45 minutes. Each repetition costs 3 additional minutes even before overhead. Repeating this unchanged workflow will not create a time saving.


Method / Check the assumptions
The calculation is deliberately simple.
Let N be repetitions, M usual effort, A assisted preparation and production, R review and repair per task, S setup, and K total upkeep for the window. All time inputs use minutes.
Usual total = N × M
Assisted total = S + K + N × (A + R)
Net time saved = N × (M - A - R) - S - K
When the per-task difference M - A - R is positive, the first repetition with no net time loss is the ceiling of (S + K) divided by that difference, with at least one repetition. Strictly positive savings start one whole repetition beyond the floor of that ratio. A result of zero is break-even, not a saving.
Both thresholds hold setup and upkeep fixed. They are not a prediction of calendar time. If more repetitions require extra maintenance, or if task difficulty changes, enter a new comparison. The calculator uses integer hundredths of minutes so exact break-even does not depend on binary decimal rounding.
How a small assumption changes the decision
Fictional repeated-task example: With 30 minutes usually, 8 minutes assisted production, 7 minutes review, six repetitions, 60 minutes setup and 15 minutes upkeep, the assisted workflow saves 15 minutes. With the same production and overhead but 10 minutes of review instead of 7, it costs 3 minutes more than the usual workflow. Review time is not a trivial footnote: 6 × 3 = 18 additional minutes, enough to reverse the original 15-minute advantage.
At these inputs, the largest review budget that still breaks even is 9.5 minutes per repetition. Keep this separate from the quality check: a shorter workflow that fails your acceptance standard is not an acceptable substitute. The new result explanation supplies a proposed next step and a hypothetical 2-minute review stress test; neither is a prediction or a measured result.


What these numbers cannot tell you
Time is only one cost. Subscription fees, cognitive effort, enjoyment, privacy, reliability, and the effects on other people are not converted into a score. A workflow that fails the acceptance standard is not an equivalent replacement, even when its time result is positive.
For observations, keep comparable tasks and include failed attempts. A simple before/after comparison is not a controlled experiment and cannot isolate whether AI caused a change. Label estimates as estimates and revisit them after doing the work. Read Did the tool actually make life easier? for the broader decision.

Compare the same work at the same acceptable quality. Use a consistent
measure of effort. Count waiting only when it prevents other useful work;

Usual total = N * M
Assisted total = S + K + N * (A + R)
Net time saved = N * (M - A - R) - S - K

If M - A - R is positive, no net time loss begins at the ceiling of
(S + K) / (M - A - R), with at least one repetition.
Strictly positive savings begin at floor((S + K) / (M - A - R)) + 1.
These thresholds hold setup and upkeep fixed. Recalculate if they grow.
